standard.title: Multiplication and division strategies
standard.description: multiply and divide one- and two-digit numbers, representing problems using number sentences, diagrams and arrays, and using a variety of calculation strategies
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can multiply and divide by one-digit numbers using repeated addition, equal grouping, arrays and partitioning (AC9M2N05). They have not yet extended multiplication to two-digit numbers, or represented multiplicative problems using formal number sentences and arrays systematically.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students multiply and divide one- and two-digit numbers, using number sentences, diagrams and arrays to represent and solve problems with a variety of calculation strategies.

nodes.label: Multiplication representations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent a multiplication situation as an array, a repeated addition and a number sentence, connecting all three.
nodes.minimum_width: Represent one multiplication fact in three ways: array, repeated addition, and number sentence. Explain the connection between representations.
nodes.typical_width: Represent a range of multiplication situations using arrays, repeated addition and number sentences; explain how all three representations show the same quantity.
wider: Explore commutativity through arrays — rotating an array shows the same product, connecting 3×4 and 4×3 as the same area
Investigate multiplication in First Nations Australian contexts such as equal-sharing of resources or pattern-based counting

response_modes.reason: Students who see multiplication only as repeated addition often struggle to transition to arrays and then to formal strategies. Connecting across representations early prevents this bottleneck.

nodes.hinge_reason: Array and number sentence representations are the entry point for Node 2 strategies (partitioning, doubling use arrays as structural models) and Node 3 (division connected to multiplication via arrays). Students who cannot flexibly move between representations cannot access the strategy-building and inverse-relationship work in subsequent nodes.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Commutativity through arrays is genuinely rich — students discover a structural property of multiplication rather than memorising a rule, which supports long-term multiplicative reasoning.
success_criteria: Students can draw an array for a given multiplication number sentence.
Students can write a multiplication number sentence for a given array or equal groups scenario.

nodes.label: Multiplication strategies for one- and two-digit numbers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can multiply a one-digit number by a two-digit number using at least one efficient strategy (e.g. partitioning, doubling).
nodes.minimum_width: Calculate at least three products involving a two-digit number using a chosen strategy, recording working.
nodes.typical_width: Apply and compare partitioning, doubling-and-halving and repeated addition strategies to multiply one-digit by two-digit numbers; choose an efficient strategy for a given problem.
wider: Explore the area model as a visual representation of two-digit multiplication (e.g. 4×23 as a 4×20 + 4×3 rectangle)
Investigate patterns in multiplication tables, using the area model to explain why the pattern holds

response_modes.reason: Building a repertoire of strategies — partitioning, doubling, using known facts — is the explicit goal of this descriptor. Students need to have encountered enough strategy examples to make genuine choices.

success_criteria: Students can calculate a one-digit by two-digit product using at least one named strategy.
Students can explain the strategy they used and why it works.

nodes.label: Division as the inverse of multiplication
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent a division problem using a number sentence and array, and connect it to the related multiplication fact.
nodes.minimum_width: Solve two division problems by connecting to a known multiplication fact; represent each as a number sentence.
nodes.typical_width: Solve a range of division problems by relating them to multiplication; represent using diagrams, number sentences and sharing/grouping models.
wider: Explore the distinction between sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) division contexts, recognising both produce the same calculation
Investigate remainders — what happens when division does not produce a whole number result

response_modes.reason: Students often treat division as a separate topic from multiplication. Seeing division in both sharing and grouping contexts, each connected to multiplication arrays, resolves this fragmentation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The partitive vs quotitive division distinction and the introduction of remainders provide genuine conceptual richness for advancing students — these are ideas that recur throughout upper primary mathematics.
success_criteria: Students can write a division number sentence for a sharing or grouping problem.
Students can use a multiplication fact to solve a related division problem.
